data.current_role: Founder of the David Horowitz Freedom Center (died April 29, 2025)
data.summary: David Horowitz (1939–2025) was an American writer and activist who moved from the New Left, where he co-edited Ramparts magazine and worked with the Black Panther Party, to the conservative movement. In 1988 he and Peter Collier founded the Center for the Study of Popular Culture, later renamed the David Horowitz Freedom Center, which published FrontPage Magazine and campaigned on campus politics and against what it called Islamist radicalism; critics, including the Southern Poverty Law Center, accused it of anti-Muslim bigotry. He was a longtime mentor to Stephen Miller. He died on April 29, 2025, at 86.

data.current_role: 47th President of the United States (since January 20, 2025)
data.summary: Donald Trump (born 1946) is the 47th president of the United States, in office since January 20, 2025, and was also the 45th president (2017–2021), the second president to serve non-consecutive terms. A New York real estate developer who ran his family's business, renamed the Trump Organization, and hosted NBC's The Apprentice from 2004, he was impeached twice in his first term and acquitted both times. In May 2024 a New York jury convicted him on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records; he was sentenced to an unconditional discharge. data.current_role: CEO of Tesla and of SpaceX (which absorbed xAI in February 2026 and went public in June 2026)
data.summary: Elon Musk co-founded X.com in 1999, which merged with Confinity to form PayPal; he was replaced as CEO in 2000 but was its largest shareholder when eBay bought it. He founded SpaceX in 2002, became Tesla's chairman in 2004 and CEO in 2008, bought Twitter in 2022 (renamed X), and merged his AI company xAI into SpaceX in 2026 ahead of a record IPO. He spent at least $250 million backing Trump in 2024, led DOGE in 2025, then feuded publicly with Trump before returning to fund Republicans in the 2026 midterms.

data.current_role: U.S. Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs (since October 16, 2025)
data.summary: Jacob Helberg is the State Department’s Under Secretary for Economic Affairs, where he launched Pax Silica, a U.S.-led pact on AI and critical-mineral supply chains. Before that he led Google’s global policy work against foreign interference, served on the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission (2022–2024), advised Palantir CEO Alex Karp, wrote The Wires of War (2021) and co-founded the Hill & Valley Forum. A Democratic donor in 2020, he gave $1 million to back Trump in 2024; he is married to investor Keith Rabois.

data.current_role: Former U.S. Attorney General (2017–2018) and former U.S. Senator from Alabama (1997–2017)
data.summary: Jeff Sessions is an Alabama Republican who served as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Alabama, Alabama attorney general, U.S. senator from 1997 to 2017, and the 84th U.S. Attorney General from 2017 to 2018. He was the first senator to endorse Donald Trump in 2016, but his recusal from the Russia investigation led to a public rift; he resigned at Trump's request in November 2018 and lost the 2020 Alabama Senate Republican runoff to the Trump-endorsed Tommy Tuberville. A 1986 nomination to the federal bench was rejected by the Senate Judiciary Committee.

data.name: Jeffrey Epstein
data.current_role: Financier and convicted sex offender (died August 10, 2019)
data.summary: Jeffrey Epstein was a New York financier who managed money for wealthy clients, chiefly retail billionaire Les Wexner, and cultivated ties with prominent figures in politics, business and academia. He pleaded guilty in Florida in 2008 to state charges including soliciting a minor for prostitution, was arrested on federal sex-trafficking charges in July 2019, and died in a Manhattan jail on August 10, 2019, in a death ruled a suicide. Congress ordered the release of the government’s Epstein files in November 2025, and the Justice Department published about 3.5 million pages in January 2026.

connections.name: Donald Trump
connections.description: Trump and Epstein socialized from the late 1980s into the early 2000s; in a 2002 New York magazine profile Trump said he had known Epstein for 15 years and called him a “terrific guy,” and flight logs entered at Ghislaine Maxwell’s 2021 trial show Trump on Epstein’s plane several times between 1993 and 1997. Public sightings ended around 2004, when they bid against each other for a Palm Beach mansion; Trump has said they had a falling out, that he threw Epstein out of Mar-a-Lago and “wasn’t a fan.” In July 2025 Trump sued the Wall Street Journal over its report of a 2003 birthday letter it attributed to him, which he denies writing.

data.summary: Kari Lake was a Phoenix TV news anchor at KSAZ (Fox 10) from 1999 to 2021, then a Trump-endorsed Republican nominee who lost the 2022 Arizona governor's race to Katie Hobbs, refused to concede and lost a two-year court challenge, and lost the 2024 Senate race to Ruben Gallego. Trump picked her to lead Voice of America; as a USAGM adviser and, from July to November 2025, its acting CEO she drove mass layoffs, and in March 2026 a federal judge ruled her acting tenure unlawful and voided those actions. In May 2026 Trump nominated her ambassador to Jamaica; the Senate Foreign Relations Committee approved her 12–10 in July, and the nomination was still awaiting a full Senate vote on the Senate's September 30, 2026 executive calendar.

He has not been charged with any crime.

data.summary: Marco Rubio is a Florida Republican who was Speaker of the Florida House (2006–2008) and a U.S. senator (2011–2025). He co-wrote the 2013 bipartisan Gang of Eight immigration bill, which Jeff Sessions led the fight against, and ran for president in 2016 against Donald Trump. Confirmed 99–0 as secretary of state on Trump's first day back in office, he also took over as national security adviser in May 2025, the first person to hold both jobs since Henry Kissinger.

data.current_role: Professor of political science, University of Notre Dame

data.current_role: U.S. Secretary of Defense, styled Secretary of War (since January 25, 2025)
data.summary: Pete Hegseth, a Princeton graduate and Army National Guard officer who served at Guantánamo Bay, in Iraq and in Afghanistan, led the advocacy groups Vets for Freedom and Concerned Veterans for America and was a Fox News contributor and host from 2014 to 2024. Trump chose him as defense secretary; the Senate confirmed him 51–50 on January 24, 2025, with JD Vance breaking the tie, and since September 2025 he also uses the title Secretary of War. He has overseen strikes on alleged drug boats from September 2025, the war with Iran that began on February 28, 2026, and the 2026 designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk. Rep. Thomas Massie filed impeachment articles against him in September 2026, and after Republicans lost Congress in November 2026 Trump said Hegseth would stay while reports said he was weighing a replacement.

data.summary: Rebekah Mercer (born 1973), a Stanford-trained former trader at Renaissance Technologies, runs the political and philanthropic giving of her father Robert Mercer. She led the pro-Cruz super PAC in 2016, then helped install Steve Bannon and Kellyanne Conway in Trump's campaign and served on his transition executive committee. She co-founded and controls the social network Parler, broke with Bannon in 2018, and is reported as a co-founder of the venture firm 1789 Capital with Omeed Malik and Chris Buskirk, where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner.

data.current_role: Former co-CEO of Renaissance Technologies; Republican megadonor
data.summary: Robert Mercer is a computer scientist who helped pioneer statistical machine translation at IBM before joining the hedge fund Renaissance Technologies in 1993, becoming co-CEO in 2009. With his daughter Rebekah he built a network of right-wing institutions: he was a major funder of Breitbart News, majority owner of Cambridge Analytica's parent SCL Group, and a top backer of Ted Cruz and then Donald Trump in 2016, helping place Steve Bannon and Kellyanne Conway in Trump's campaign. Under scrutiny he stepped down from Renaissance and sold his Breitbart stake to his daughters in November 2017, scaling back his giving before returning to back Trump in 2020 and 2024.

They met when Miller, as a Santa Monica High student, campaigned to bring Horowitz to speak at the school; at Duke, Miller led a chapter of Horowitz's Students for Academic Freedom. Horowitz says he recommended Miller for jobs with Rep. Michele Bachmann, Rep. John Shadegg and then Sen. Jeff Sessions. Miller praised Horowitz's legacy when he died in April 2025.

data.summary: Yoram Hazony is an Israeli-American philosopher and political theorist, born in Israel in 1964 and raised in the US. Not in the links: token sales of about $550 million by March 2025 (Bloomberg); an OCC preliminary conditional approval on August 14, 2026 for World Liberty Trust Company, a national trust bank to issue USD1 (Crowdfund Insider; application per The Block); a WLFI buyback announced in November 2026 after the token fell more than 60% in 2026 (Reuters via Investing.com); and House Democrats’ plans to investigate it when they take control of the Oversight Committee in 2027 (crypto.news, Bankless). updates.text: 44 ties that rested on a single source now have a second, independent one, mostly official records (presidential libraries, embassy and Senate pages, FEC filings, the Congressional Record) or reporting from outlets on both sides. Fixed: on phones the map no longer opens or closes things on its own while you move around. A tap now counts only when your finger barely moves, so pans, pinches and small nudges select nothing; taps land on the nearest person instead of a stray line; nothing lights up unless you tap it; and tapping empty map folds the details sheet down instead of closing it (use × or swipe down to close).

New: Views → Factions & rifts. Factions sorts the map into nine blocs from who is allied with and feuding with whom, among them Trump's inner circle, a JD Vance and donor bloc, a Donald Trump Jr. and Tucker Carlson bloc, the PayPal Mafia, national conservatives, Middle East dealmakers and the Harris-led Democrats, with the feuds between them and the people who bridge them. Rift watch ranks friendly ties showing strains that came before past breaks: a friend of one feuding with the other, rival 2028 ambitions, a recent request turned down, an old feud. Tested on ties frozen at 2020, 2022 and 2024, the five that later broke (including Trump and DeSantis, and Trump and Musk) scored above 82% of those that held, though five is a small test. Top of the list now: Trump and Bannon, Vance and Rubio, Ken Griffin and DeSantis. A pair's panel shows its warning.

New: a track record in each person's Pull tab, listing 28 sourced asks of officials (appointments, policy, contracts, rulings, disaster aid) and how they turned out. Tested against them, overall Pull did not predict who got their way (a coin flip), while closeness to the official who decided did, modestly; Pull's weights stay as they are, and a denied ask never lowers anyone's score. Also new: freshness checks. The org chart flags posts not confirmed in 30 days, the Record tab shows how old each file's research is, and the weekly refresh now confirms posts that are due, re-runs the FEC import, logs predictions and saves a monthly snapshot for trend arrows.

Campaign finance filings imported from the FEC for 44 donors, 2016 to 2026: about 18,000 itemized gifts, matched by name and employer so namesakes are left out, with no addresses kept. Each donor's Money tab now lists who they funded cycle by cycle, with links to the filings, and gifts of $10,000 or more to someone on the map became 106 new money lines. Where filings and news reports disagree, both figures show. With four times as many past donations to test on, the 2028 backing score still holds up: 0.80 and 0.88 (0.50 is a coin flip), and about 6 in 10 pairs it rates likely went on to give.

New: 2028 backing (Views, and a 2028 tab on each person). It predicts who is likely to back each contender from how close they are and how well their politics fit, on top of declared camps and reported plans. On past donations it beat closeness alone (0.88 against 0.82 for the 2026 cycle), and about 6 in 10 pairs it rated likely went on to give. Today it has 219 predictions outside the camps, led by JD Vance (68), Marco Rubio (60) and Donald Trump Jr. (55); all are saved in a dated log to be checked later. People who have died (David Horowitz, Jeffrey Epstein) no longer appear in the Pull ranking.

Certainty is now earned from sources: a tie resting on one news story counts for at most 80%, on Wikipedia alone 75%, and only an official record or two independent outlets carry it in full. Single-source ties are drawn dashed and marked in the details. 31 files gained second sources or official pages, and a post's own record now backs the job, so single-source ties fell from 222 to 181 of 909. A new scorecard freezes the map at a past year and tests its predictions: closeness picks out future ties (0.76 against 0.70 for the best simple baseline, where 0.50 is a coin flip) and next-cycle donations (0.82 against 0.75 for "same as last time").
